title: 2020 Continuous-time state-space modelling of the hot hand in basketball
file_name: 2020 Continuous-time state-space modelling of the hot hand in basketball.pdf
universal_lens: Continuous-time state-space models unify irregularly sampled free throw data with latent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics to detect hot hand serial dependence. Continuous-time state-space models with Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics enable probabilistic inference over latent shooting states in basketball, bridging stochastic processes and Bayesian decision theory.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference on latent player form via continuous-time SSMs enables probabilistic hot hand detection with conformal uncertainty quantification. Bayesian inference framework applied to discrete-time Bernoulli observations within a continuous-state hidden Markov model using approximate likelihood maximization.
gse_mapping: Situationally-aware state transitions model player form evolution; stochastic dynamics govern performance fluctuations across game time. Situational reasoning engine maps player shooting states through time-varying transitions governed by OU process dynamics, enabling real-time tactical adaptation.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 1 introduces a continuous-time state-space model to analyze the hot hand phenomenon in basketball through 110,513 free throw attempts. The core innovation lies in modeling player form as a latent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, capturing how performance varies over time. This approach addresses the irregular sampling nature of free throws within games, unlike traditional discrete-time methods. The model assumes that each shot outcome depends on an unobserved but evolving player state—form—which reverts toward a long-term average. By applying Bayesian inference, the framework estimates the strength of the hot hand effect, finding support for its existence albeit with a modest magnitude. This aligns with prior literature where Gilovich et al. (1985) dismissed the phenomenon due to perceived cognitive biases, yet subsequent studies including this one suggest otherwise. The methodological shift towards continuous-time modeling allows for more nuanced temporal dynamics compared to earlier experiments relying on fixed trials. It also provides a principled way to incorporate irregular timing into statistical inference, making it suitable for real-world sports data analysis. reasoning_traces.think: This chapter introduces a sophisticated continuous-time state-space model for analyzing the hot hand phenomenon in basketball. It employs an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process to describe latent shooting states that evolve over time, assuming each player's state follows a normal distribution with mean zero and variance σ²/(2θ). Observations are modeled as Bernoulli trials dependent on these latent states and additional covariates such as game context. The key innovation lies in approximating the intractable multidimensional integral involved in computing the likelihood by discretizing the continuous state space—a technique rooted in hidden Markov models. This allows for efficient computation using algorithms like the forward algorithm. Parameters are estimated via numerical maximization of the approximate joint likelihood, ensuring consistency and unbiasedness. Empirical results show strong support for the presence of a hot hand effect, as evidenced by significant information criterion improvements over baseline models without latent states. The model thus provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for understanding dynamic performance fluctuations in sports.
